description: Poseidon's Trident is the iconic three-pronged spear or scepter wielded by the Greek god of the sea, Poseidon. More than just a weapon, it is a symbol of his power and authority over the marine realm, granting him control over the waves, storms, and earthquakes. Forged by the Cyclopes during the Titanomachy, the trident is an instrument of immense power, capable of stirring the seas into towering tsunamis or calming them into tranquil waters. With a flick of the wrist, Poseidon could shatter rocks, summon sea monsters, and even create freshwater springs. The trident is not merely an object of brute force, but also a representation of Poseidon's volatile temperament and dominion over the unpredictable nature of the sea. Its three prongs are often interpreted as representing the three aspects of Poseidon's rule: the sea, the earth (earthquakes), and the underworld (as Poseidon was sometimes associated with subterranean realms). In artistic depictions, the trident is frequently shown alongside Poseidon's chariot, dolphins, and other marine creatures, reinforcing his identity as the quintessential sea god. The loss or theft of the trident would signify a grave disruption in the natural order, potentially unleashing chaos and devastation upon both land and sea. It represents the untamed and often destructive force of the ocean, a power that only Poseidon can fully control.

shortDescription: The Three-Pronged Scepter of the Sea Lord
subtitle: The tool of storms, earthquakes, and oceanic dominion.

keyMyths.title: The Creation of a Spring
keyMyths.description: During the contest for patronage of Athens, Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident, creating a saltwater spring. Although impressive, Athena's gift of an olive tree was deemed more valuable by the Athenians, and she won the patronage.

keyMyths.title: The Walls of Troy
keyMyths.description: Poseidon, along with Apollo, was forced to serve King Laomedon of Troy. They built the great walls of the city, but Laomedon refused to pay them their due, incurring Poseidon's wrath and leading to the Trojan War.

keyMyths.title: The Wrath Against Odysseus
keyMyths.description: After Odysseus blinded Polyphemus, Poseidon, the cyclops' father, relentlessly pursued Odysseus with his trident, stirring up storms and shipwrecks to prevent his return home to Ithaca for ten long years.

keyMyths.title: The Contest with Athena at Troezen
keyMyths.description: Similar to the contest at Athens, Poseidon and Athena vied for patronage of Troezen. Poseidon offered a saltwater spring, while Athena offered the olive tree. The gods decided they should share the patronage.

keyMyths.title: Quelling the Storm for Aeneas
keyMyths.description: In Virgil's *Aeneid*, Neptune (Roman equivalent of Poseidon) uses his trident to calm the storm Juno created to hinder Aeneas' journey to Italy, demonstrating his power over the seas.

extendedContent.content:
The Trident of Poseidon stands as one of the most recognizable divine weapons
                    in Greek mythology, the three-pronged spear that symbolizes the sea god's
                    dominion over the oceans, earthquakes, and horses. This mighty weapon is
                    inseparable from Poseidon's identity - in virtually every ancient depiction,
                    the god holds his trident as both weapon and scepter of his underwater kingdom.
                
                
                    The trident's three prongs represent Poseidon's threefold domain: the surface
                    of the sea, its depths, and the creatures within it. Some interpretations
                    connect the prongs to past, present, and future, or to birth, life, and death
                    as they relate to the sea's power to give and take life.
                
                
                    As a symbol, the trident transcended Greek religion to become a universal
                    emblem of maritime power. Roman Neptune inherited the weapon along with
                    Poseidon's attributes, and the trident remains associated with naval imagery
                    to this day.
extendedContent.title: Description and Nature

extendedContent.content:
Forged by the Cyclopes
                
                    The trident was forged by the Elder Cyclopes - Brontes (Thunder), Steropes
                    (Lightning), and Arges (Brightness) - during the Titanomachy, the great war
                    between the Olympian gods and the Titans. These three sons of Uranus and
                    Gaia had been imprisoned in Tartarus by Cronus but were freed by Zeus to
                    aid the Olympians.
                
                
                    In gratitude and as weapons for the war, the Cyclopes forged three divine
                    instruments: the thunderbolt for Zeus, the helm of invisibility for Hades,
                    and the trident for Poseidon. These weapons proved decisive in the Olympians'
                    victory, each embodying dominion over a realm of the cosmos.
                

                Symbol of Cosmic Division
                
                    After the Titans' defeat, the three brothers - Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades -
                    divided the universe among themselves. Zeus received the sky, Hades the
                    underworld, and Poseidon the seas. The trident became both weapon and
                    symbol of Poseidon's sovereignty over his watery domain, just as the
                    thunderbolt represented Zeus's rule of the heavens.
extendedContent.title: Origin and the Titanomachy

extendedContent.content:
The Contest for Athens
                
                    When Poseidon and Athena competed for patronage of the city that would
                    become Athens, both offered gifts. Poseidon struck the Acropolis with
                    his trident, producing either a saltwater spring or (in some versions)
                    the first horse. Athena offered the olive tree. The citizens chose
                    Athena's gift, and Poseidon's anger at losing caused him to flood the
                    Thriasian plain.
                

                The Odyssey
                
                    Throughout the Odyssey, Poseidon uses his trident's powers to torment
                    Odysseus for blinding the Cyclops Polyphemus, Poseidon's son. The god
                    raises storms and shipwrecks that extend Odysseus's journey for years.
                

                The Trojan War
                
                    During the Trojan War, Poseidon used his trident to aid the Greeks,
                    building the walls of Troy (which he later helped destroy) and
                    intervening in various battles. His earthquake powers shook the
                    battlefield when he walked.
extendedContent.title: Famous Mythological Appearances

associations.name: Dolphins
associations.significance: Dolphins are frequent companions of Poseidon, linking the trident to beneficence.

associations.name: Warfare

cultural.modernLegacy: The trident remains a potent symbol of maritime power and is widely used in nautical emblems, fictional works, and popular culture. It is often associated with strength, authority, and the untamed forces of nature.
